metaDescription: Six large salad spinners from 6.22 quarts to 26.42 quarts, from family pump models to commercial units that dry up to eight or nine heads at once.
introParagraphs: Large salad spinners fall into two very different groups. Household models like the KitchenAid and OXO top out around 6 to 7.5 quarts and are designed to sit in a regular cabinet, while commercial units start at 10 quarts and climb past 26 quarts, with sizes measured in heads of lettuce rather than servings. Choosing between them is mostly a question of how much produce you wash and where you can store the thing.

The six picks here cover both ends. KitchenAid at 7.43 quarts, OXO at 6.22 and SveBake at 6.34 are kitchen-friendly, while GATBO at 10 quarts, CLIVIA at 20 and Fnova at 26.42 are meant for restaurants, meal prep businesses or very large households. We evaluated listing specs and design details, and we flag anything the listing does not state.
Before buying a commercial-size model, measure the space it needs and think about how you will drain and lift it, because those two points matter more than raw capacity.

products.name: KitchenAid Universal Salad Spinner, 7.43 Qt

specList.label: Extras
specList.value: Basket as colander, bowl for serving

products.description:
The KitchenAid Universal is the largest household-style spinner here at 7.43 quarts, and the listing describes a soft-touch pump with a brake button for comfortable one-handed operation. You press the pump to spin and tap the brake to stop, so one hand stays free to steady the bowl. The listing also says the basket can be used separately as a colander and the bowl can be used to serve salads.

That extra capacity means it can handle a large head of lettuce or a big family salad in one go. The listing does not give outside dimensions, so check the product page before assuming it fits under a low cabinet. A bigger plastic bowl is also lighter than steel but takes more room in a drawer or on a shelf.

Compared with the OXO at 6.22 quarts, the KitchenAid gives you about 1.2 quarts more room with a similar pump-and-brake approach. Against the SveBake at 6.34 quarts, it is larger, though the SveBake has a steel bowl. If you want the most volume without moving to commercial equipment, this is the one to start with, and it is the only pick here that pairs a household footprint with a pump and brake.

products.name: OXO Good Grips 6.22 Qt Salad Spinner
products.description:
The OXO Good Grips uses a one-touch pump, and the maker notes that OXO invented the one-touch salad spinner. The 6.22 quart bowl holds a good-sized salad without becoming a commercial piece of equipment. The listing explains that after use you can press the pump down and slide it flush to store it neatly.

The listing does not describe the brake in the text we reviewed, so check the product page if instant stopping matters. It is a plastic-bowl model, which keeps weight down but can scratch over time. For the pump to work well, the basket should be loaded evenly rather than packed tightly.

Compared with the KitchenAid at 7.43 quarts, the OXO is smaller but more compact on a shelf, and its flush-lock pump helps stacking. Against the SveBake at 6.34 quarts, it is roughly the same volume with a plastic bowl and a pump rather than a locking steel lid. Compared with GATBO at 10 quarts, it holds less than half as much, which is the tradeoff for a bowl that fits an ordinary cabinet.
products.bestFor: Households that want a large spinner that still stores in a normal cabinet.
pros: One-handed pump is easy on the hands
Bowl and strainer separate to wash
cons: Plastic bowl can scratch over time
Brake details not stated in the listing

products.name: SveBake Stainless Steel Salad Spinner, 6.34 Qt
products.description:
The SveBake 6.34 quart spinner combines a stainless steel bowl with a locking lid that the listing says keeps the cover from flying off or slipping during spinning. The steel is described as sturdy, durable and resistant, so it suits buyers who want to avoid plastic staining. The 6.34 quart size handles a variety of fruits and vegetables.

The listing excerpt does not say how the basket is driven, whether by pump, crank or knob, so check the product page before ordering. That detail matters because a crank needs both hands and a pump needs one. A steel bowl is also heavier than plastic and opaque, so you cannot see the water level.

Compared with the KitchenAid at 7.43 quarts, it is about 1.1 quarts smaller but gives you steel instead of plastic. Against the OXO at 6.22 quarts, it is nearly the same capacity with a locking lid in place of a pump-and-flush design. Compared with GATBO at 10 quarts, it is far smaller but fits a normal kitchen, which makes it a reasonable choice if you want durable materials without commercial size.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a large steel-bowl spinner with a lid that locks.
cons: Spin mechanism not stated in the listing
Heavier and opaque compared with plastic

products.name: GATBO Commercial Salad Spinner, 10 Qt
products.description:
GATBO is a commercial-style 10 quart (2.5 gallon) spinner, and the listing says it dries three to four heads of lettuce per cycle. It is made from food-grade polypropylene with BPA-free construction, and the listing mentions a sealed gearbox that helps prevent water ingress. That gear protection is the key difference from consumer pump spinners.

The listing targets restaurants, cafes and home kitchens, which makes it a reasonable step up for someone who meal-preps or catering at home. A 10 quart unit is still a big object, so expect it to live on a shelf or in a pantry. The listing text we reviewed does not describe the handle length or drain method, so check the product page.

Compared with the KitchenAid at 7.43 quarts, GATBO holds about 2.6 quarts more and is built for repeated daily use. Against CLIVIA at 20 quarts, it is half the size, which is far easier to lift and store. Compared with the OXO at 6.22 quarts, it handles roughly one and a half times the volume. It is the best bridge between home and commercial capacity.
products.bestFor: Small food businesses or heavy home meal-preppers who need up to four heads at once.
cons: Too big for a standard cabinet
Drain and handle details not stated

products.name: CLIVIA Commercial Salad Spinner, 20 Qt
products.description:
CLIVIA is a 20 quart (5 gallon) manual commercial spinner, and the title says it dries up to seven heads of lettuce while a spec line mentions up to eight. The listing gives the dimensions as 18.3 by 22.24 inches and says it has 304 bearing shafts and a brake device that safely stops the bucket. That brake is important at this size, because a heavy spinning basket takes time to wind down.

It is a huge piece of equipment for a household, so measure counter and shelf space before ordering. Moving the unit around when full of wet lettuce is awkward, so think about where it will sit. The listing does not describe a drain tube in the excerpt, so check the product page for drainage details.

Compared with GATBO at 10 quarts, it doubles the volume, and against the Fnova at 26.42 quarts it is a bit smaller and lacks the long drain tube noted in the Fnova listing. Compared with the KitchenAid at 7.43 quarts, it is nearly three times the size. It suits restaurants and caterers, and it is overkill for a typical home.
products.bestFor: Restaurants and caterers that wash several heads of lettuce at once.
pros: 20 quart capacity handles up to 7 heads
cons: Very large to store and lift
Drain details not in the excerpt

products.name: Fnova Commercial Salad Spinner, 26.42 Qt
products.description:
Fnova is the largest spinner in this group at 6.6 gallons or 26.42 quarts, and the listing says it can spin eight to nine heads of lettuce at once. A 4.92 foot (1.5 m) drain tube directs water straight to a sink or floor drain, which means you do not have to lift the heavy bowl to empty it. Anti-slip feet help keep the machine steady while spinning.

The manual spinning mechanism is described as powerful, but at this scale you will be turning a heavy basket of wet produce, so strength matters. The listing does not give a weight, so check the product page. This is a tool for high-volume prep, and a household would rarely need it.

Compared with CLIVIA at 20 quarts, the Fnova adds about 6.4 quarts and a drain tube, which are the main reasons to pay for it. Against GATBO at 10 quarts, it is more than two and a half times the volume. Compared with the KitchenAid at 7.43 quarts, it is in a different class entirely, so choose it only if you really wash that much.
products.bestFor: High-volume kitchens that want a long drain tube and the biggest capacity.
pros: 4.92 ft drain tube avoids lifting water
cons: Far too big for most homes

buyingCriteria.explanation: A household spinner tops out around 7.43 quarts like the KitchenAid, while commercial units start at 10 quarts with GATBO and climb to 26.42 quarts with Fnova. Commercial models are rated in heads of lettuce, from 3 to 4 on GATBO to 8 to 9 on Fnova. If you cook for a family, a home model is enough. Only choose commercial size if you routinely wash many heads at once.

Capacity means nothing if the spinner will not fit. CLIVIA measures 18.3 by 22.24 inches, which is larger than most countertop appliances. Household picks like the OXO 6.22 quart and KitchenAid 7.43 quart fit in a cabinet, while commercial ones need a pantry shelf or floor space. Measure before ordering, and leave room to lift the lid.

Lifting a bowl of wet water is the worst part of a large spinner. The Fnova solves this with a 4.92 foot drain tube that leads water to a sink or floor drain. The other commercial picks do not mention a tube in the text we reviewed, so check each product page. For household models, a bowl you can carry to the sink is fine.

Large baskets store momentum, so a brake matters. The KitchenAid has a brake button and soft-touch pump, and CLIVIA has a brake device that safely stops the bucket. A pump leaves a hand free, while a crank on heavy commercial units usually needs both hands. If you will use the unit daily, favor a brake and a smooth drive.

At commercial scale, gears and shafts take real stress. GATBO lists a sealed gearbox to keep water out, and CLIVIA lists 304 bearing shafts. Household models rely on lighter mechanisms, so expect shorter life under heavy use. If you spin daily, durable internals are worth more than extra capacity.

Plastic bowls like the OXO and KitchenAid are lighter, while the SveBake 6.34 quart has a stainless steel bowl that resists stains. GATBO uses food-grade polypropylene. Large bowls need room in the sink to wash, so check the diameter before buying. Take everything apart and dry the gear area to avoid mildew.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity and real use
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared capacity from the OXO at 6.22 quarts up to the Fnova at 26.42 quarts and translated it into heads of lettuce where the listing did so. GATBO handles 3 to 4 heads, CLIVIA up to 7 and Fnova 8 to 9. Larger models were not automatically ranked higher, since they are impractical for most kitchens.

howWeEvaluated.title: Storage and footprint
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at listed dimensions and how each spinner stores. The CLIVIA lists 18.3 by 22.24 inches, while the OXO has a pump that locks flush for compact storage. Household models score better for ordinary cabinets, and commercial ones were judged for pantry or kitchen floor use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Drainage and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked whether the listing describes a drain tube or easy water removal. The Fnova leads with its 4.92 foot tube, and anti-slip feet help with stability. For household models we considered how easy the bowl is to carry to the sink.

howWeEvaluated.title: Mechanism and durability
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted gear protection and bearings, such as the sealed gearbox on GATBO and 304 bearing shafts on CLIVIA. The KitchenAid and OXO lean on pumps and brakes, which suit home use. Anything not stated, such as the SveBake drive, was flagged.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value of the lineup
howWeEvaluated.description: We positioned each pick, with KitchenAid and OXO leading home use, SveBake leading steel bowls, GATBO bridging to commercial, and CLIVIA and Fnova covering high volume. Each pick has a clear use rather than overlapping with the others.

faq.q: What is the largest salad spinner I can use at home?
faq.a: The KitchenAid at 7.43 quarts is the largest household-style model here and fits in a normal cabinet. Anything above that, like GATBO at 10 quarts, is commercial. Check space first.

faq.q: How many heads of lettuce can a large spinner dry?
faq.a: It depends on size. GATBO lists 3 to 4 heads, CLIVIA up to 7 or 8, and Fnova 8 to 9. Home models like the OXO at 6.22 quarts handle one large head.

faq.q: Are commercial salad spinners worth it for home use?
faq.a: Only if you cook for crowds or meal prep in bulk. They are heavy, large and hard to store. For most homes, a 6 to 7.5 quart model is enough.

faq.q: Do I need a drain tube?
faq.a: It helps at very large sizes because lifting a full bowl is awkward. The Fnova lists a 4.92 foot tube, while others do not mention one in our excerpt. Check the product page for drain details.

faq.q: Plastic or stainless steel for a large spinner?
faq.a: Plastic is lighter and see-through, as with the OXO and KitchenAid. Stainless steel on the SveBake resists stains but is heavier. Pick based on how often you carry it.

faq.q: How do I stop a large basket quickly?
faq.a: Use a brake, such as the button on the KitchenAid or the brake device on CLIVIA. Never stop the basket with your hand. Let it slow before opening the lid.

faq.q: How should I clean a big spinner?
faq.a: Separate the bowl, basket and lid and wash each, then dry the gear area thoroughly. Large pieces may not fit in a dishwasher, so check the product page. Dry fully before storing to avoid mildew.
